newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS - Thai finance firms struggle to raise funds.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Thai finance firms struggle to raise funds.

text.p: Cash-strapped Thai finance firms, squeezed by low liquidity and declining confidence in their stability, are borrowing at painfully high interest rates in a bid to attract funding.

Analysts said medium and small finance firms had in the past few weeks adopted an unsustainable practice of paying 20-25 percent interest on overnight funding as problems in the non-bank financial sector mount.
Few analysts could predict how long Thailand's 91 finance and securities firms, especially those without bank affiliation, could continue their high-cost funding without direct government bailouts.

"It cannot be sustained. It is a ludicrous situation that the government pledges to guarantee all public deposits raised by finance companies," said Mike Stead, head of research at Union Securities Plc.

The Bank of Thailand, in an attempt to calm public concern over the finance sector's health, said in early April that it guaranteed public funds mobilised by 10 finance firms facing cashflow problems.
The 10 companies were ordered to raise capital and to consolidate through mergers.
The central bank's guarantee, designed to forestall public runs on deposits in these firms, was understood by the market to also cover deposits at other finance companies.
The bank last week issued a circular instructing finance firms to file weekly reports detailing interest rates paid by their call promissory notes.
"I cannot imagine these high-cost funds could be re-lent to business borrowers at even higher rates," Stead said.
The overnight inter-finance rate has hovered at 17-22 percent for the past two months, about double the average interbank rate.
A fund manager at a medium-sized finance firm offered to pay 16 percent interest for a minimum 10 million baht ($416,000) by issuing call promissory notes.
"We are forced to pay higher rates as tight liquidity has given clients with surplus funds more bargaining power to shop around for higher rates," she said.

Analysts said non-bank affiliated finance firms found it tough to raise public funds or retain earlier credit lines from commercial banks amid growing market concern that their huge non-performing loans to the troubled property sector pushed some finance firms to the verge of collapse.

Supavat Saichua of Krungthai Thanakit Plc said the sector's funding problems were aggravated by Thailand's new two-tier baht exchange rate system which prompted foreign banks to withdraw previous credit lines for major Thai finance firms.
"They are taking a cautious approach, being confused about what exchange rate they would get when their loans are repaid by Thai finance firms," he said.

Analysts expected the crunch time for finance companies would come next month when they, along with commercial banks, are required for the first time to detail their non-performing and sub-standard loans.
"The extent of these non-performing loans could trigger a panic when people see it," an analyst said.
A foreign bank dealer said she this week quoted a high 19 percent rate for her overnight surplus funds to the interfinance market, hoping no finance firms would take the offer.

Money market dealers said, however, that not all finance companies were short of funds. They said major finance firms affiliated to banks had been net lenders in recent weeks, having benefited from a flight of funds from small to big firms. ($ = 24 Thai Baht)
